articles.title: Anthropic's listing bonanza: Over 5,000 employees become millionaires overnight
articles.summary: Anthropic made a blockbuster debut on Wall Street on Thursday (local time), with its valuation touching $2 trillion and the stock ending its first trading
articles.body: Anthropic made a blockbuster debut on Wall Street on Thursday (local time), with its valuation touching $2 trillion and the stock ending its first trading session nearly 17% higher.But the listing brought an even bigger windfall for the company's employees. Anthropic's remarkable journey from a small artificial intelligence startup to one of the world's most valuable companies has turned nearly its entire workforce into millionaires on paper, with some employees holding fortunes worth hundreds of millions of dollars.Priced at $83 per share, the IPO has created thousands of paper millionaires, spanning early researchers and engineers to administrative staff who received stock grants as the company expanded. Around 600 employees now have equity holdings worth more than $100 million, while nearly 5,100 staff members have shares valued at over $1 million.The scale of the employee wealth creation could make Anthropic's listing one of the biggest financial windfalls in Silicon Valley history.Over 5,000 employees get $1 millionAnthropic had a workforce of 5,300 as of September this year, according to regulatory filings. Data from Hill.com, which tracks private-company shares, shows that around 5,100 employees, or 96% of the total workforce, hold equity worth more than $1 million.The figures go much higher for a significant section of the staff. Around 2,800 employees, known internally as “Ants”, have stock holdings valued at more than $10 million. Another 600 have crossed the $100 million threshold, placing them in the “centi-millionaire” category.Andrew Benson, founder and CEO of Hill, told CNN on Thursday that the speed of this wealth creation stood out, particularly given how few employees had left the company. “What’s most surprising here is how quickly this this happened,” Benson said.He added, “It’s been pretty clear for some time that Anthropic is a rocket ship, and so it definitely discouraged people from leaving because they knew what the opportunity cost of that would be.”Anthropic's sudden riseAnthropic's employee wealth boom is closely linked to how quickly the company expanded. Founded in 2021, it had fewer than 1,000 employees at the end of 2024. By September this year, its headcount had reached 5,300.Stock-based compensation is a familiar feature of Silicon Valley startups, where companies often combine salaries with equity grants because they have limited cash to pay employees. The prospect of an eventual acquisition or IPO can also encourage employees to remain with a company until they can realise the value of their shares.But Anthropic's experience highlights how much the timing of joining a company can matter when it comes to financial returns.Benson said employees who joined earlier could end up with significantly larger gains than those who entered the company at a more senior level much later.As he put it, “being early is more important, in terms of a financial outcome, than being senior … You could be very low on the totem pole, and if you joined in 2023 or 2024, you’re likely to have a significantly better outcome than a senior person who joined earlier this year.”SpaceX comparison: Anthropic's wealth creation came much fasterThe scale of Anthropic's employee windfall can be compared with SpaceX's IPO, which created around 4,400 millionaires from a workforce of 22,000.However, SpaceX had spent more than two decades as a private company before its blockbuster listing in June. Anthropic, founded in 2021, has reached a similar milestone much earlier in its journey.The two companies also differ in how their employees are distributed. SpaceX has staff across Texas, California and Florida, while Anthropic's workforce is concentrated in San Francisco.Employees get an early opportunity to sell sharesAnthropic's IPO also stands apart because it gave non-founder insiders an opportunity to sell part of their holdings from the first day of trading.Typically, employees at companies going public must wait through a “lockup” period, which generally lasts between three and six months, before they can sell their shares.Anthropic instead introduced a complex, staggered lockup schedule that allowed non-founder insiders to cash out up to 10% of their shares as soon as trading began. However, it is not known how many employees used this option on Thursday.Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? Join the TOI Money Masterclass.

articles.title: Exclusive-US should restrict investments in China's aerospace sector, not certify Chinese aircraft, lawmakers say
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - The US government should not certify Chinese-made airplanes and pull contracts from defense contractors, including European ae...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - The US government should not certify Chinese-made airplanes and pull contracts from defense contractors, including European aerospace manufacturer Airbus, if they do not halt investments in China's aerospace industrial base, a ‌congressional report reviewed by Reuters said.

The House Select Committee on China said in a report Washington should toughen export controls ‌and restrict investments in China's aerospace sector. The report also raised concerns that Western governments did not do enough to contain the rise of China's military air ​power.

"The US and its allies should strengthen export controls and tighten investment restrictions on the aerospace sector to stop the transfer of vital technology that will empower our foremost adversary," said Representative John Moolenaar, the panel's chair and a Michigan Republican, following a year-long investigation.

The report said the FAA should not allow Chinese-manufactured aircraft to fly in the United States, noting that China has never released its report into ‌the 2022 crash of a China Eastern ⁠Airlines Boeing aircraft and citing subsidies that China has given to state-owned Chinese aircraft makers, COMAC and AVIC.

The FAA declined to comment on the report but said it has not certified any Chinese aircraft.

The US Treasury ⁠Department should restrict outbound investment into China's aerospace sector and urge allies to follow suit and subject the purchase of US aerospace companies by French firms to heightened scrutiny until they unwind ties to China's "Civil-Military Ecosystem," the report said.

The report said through joint ventures, co-development agreements, and other commercial ​relationships "American ​and other Western companies transferred technology, know-how, and industrial capacity" on aerospace ​that ultimately benefited the Chinese military.

The Chinese embassy in ‌Washington criticized the report. "China has all along opposed moves to overstretch the concept of national security or politicize trade and tech issues," the embassy said.

articles.title: Treasuries Eye Longest Rally in Five Months on Haven Demand
articles.summary: Treasuries are headed for their longest rally in almost five months, as mounting doubts over the artificial intelligence trade deepen a global stock selloff...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Treasuries are headed for their longest rally in almost five months, as mounting doubts over the artificial intelligence trade deepen a global stock selloff and drive investors toward haven assets.

Yields fell between two and three basis points across the curve in Asia on Friday, putting a gauge of Treasury returns on track for a fifth day of gains, matching the longest rally since June 29. A Bloomberg gauge of the dollar is set for its fourth straight weekly gain.

The risk-off turn is adding momentum to the Treasury rally as investors reassess lofty AI valuations and the vast spending underpinning the boom. Global stocks are poised for their longest losing streak in more than three years. With doubts over the trade spilling into broader markets, haven demand could keep yields under pressure.

"Steady falls in yields today, alongside weakness in the key Asian equity indices and US futures do point to a continuation of the risk-off moves that started overnight," said Kenneth Crompton, head of rates strategy at National Australia Bank.

Yields remain elevated despite the latest moves, with the 10-year rate nearing its longest stretch above 5% in almost two decades, reflecting concerns about sticky inflation and expectations of Federal Reserve rate hikes through next year.

While investors are wanting to cut some risk, "we don't see the AI trade as being entirely derailed," said Crompton. "The fundamental case for 10-year US Treasuries to rally well through 5% is weak."

articles.title: Can Nvidia learn from AIG's mistakes?
articles.summary: This week, the tech world is celebrating. Not only has Anthropic launched a record-breaking $81bn IPO, but Nvidia released stunning earnings...
articles.body:
This week, the tech world is celebrating. Not only has Anthropic ( ANT ) launched a record-breaking $81bn IPO , but Nvidia ( NVDA ) released stunning earnings , raising hopes that it can survive the loss of its founder, Jensen Huang.

But as champagne corks pop, investors should also note this week's financial stability report from the European Central Bank. It warns that the AI frenzy has some alarming "historical parallels with the dotcom and subprime bubbles". In particular, the ECB — like the Bank for International Settlements — frets that tech companies have amassed gigantic off-balance-sheet borrowing, creating vast, half-concealed leverage.

Silicon Valley may shrug — and/or argue that "this time is different". And nobody can deny the transformational technology that is AI.

But Nvidia fans should be paying attention. For leaving aside the macro risks, there are some uncanny micro-level parallels between the chip giant's current position and the role of the AIG ( AIG ) insurance company during the subprime mortgage bubble. And that begs a key question: can Nvidia's board learn the right lessons to avoid AIG's fate back then?

Think about it. Until the late 20th century, AIG was a stodgy behemoth. But then its hard-charging, visionary leader, Hank Greenberg, dived into credit default swaps, offering derivative contracts to help clients protect themselves against default risks.

It seemed a win-win, since AIG had a top-notch credit rating and thus could offer this protection in a cost-effective way. And so it was that AIG became a linchpin of the system, at the centre of a hairball of tightly interconnected, circular, half-concealed trades.

But then Greenberg was felled by a scandal in 2005, AIG lost its top credit rating and subprime mortgage bonds turned sour. By 2008, the insurance company had become ground zero of the credit crisis, and the government was forced to bail it out, since those interconnected flows threatened to create a systemic implosion.

There are many differences with today's Nvidia. The chipmaker has a strong, tangible core business, with cumulative net income of $183.3bn thus far, a corporate record. Its gross debt leverage is only 0.4 times, as a recent Morgan Stanley report notes.

Like AIG, Nvidia is a pillar of an ecosystem. But, although the chipmaker has provided around $100bn in equity investments and over $530bn in off-balance-sheet guarantees and lease backstops to its customers, one big difference between 2026 and 2006 is that this circular financing pattern is widely known.

articles.title: Pentagon standoff, copyright lawsuit to AI safety concerns: 5 controversies that have put Anthropic under scrutiny
articles.summary: Anthropic has positioned itself as a safety-focused alternative in an increasingly competitive AI industry, building its reputation around responsible AI
articles.body: Anthropic has positioned itself as a safety-focused alternative in an increasingly competitive AI industry, building its reputation around responsible AI development and safeguards against potential misuse.Founded by former OpenAI employees, the company has repeatedly emphasised the need to ensure that increasingly powerful AI systems remain under human control.However, its rapid rise has also brought a series of controversies, ranging from copyright infringement allegations and disagreements with the US government over military applications to concerns about the existential risks of advanced AI.The Pentagon standoffThe most high-profile dispute erupted in February 2026, when Anthropic refused to remove restrictions preventing Claude from being used for mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous lethal weapons. The US department of defence wanted broader authority to use the technology for what it called all lawful purposes.President Donald Trump directed federal agencies to stop using Anthropic’s technology, while defence secretary Pete Hegseth designated the company a national security supply-chain risk.Anthropic challenged the move in court. In September, a US appeals court upheld the Pentagon’s designation in a 2-1 decision, allowing the department to remove Claude from its systems and barring its use for Defence Department work. Anthropic said it disagreed with the appeals court ruling.$1.5 billion copyright settlementAnthropic agreed to pay $1.5 billion to settle a class-action lawsuit brought by authors who accused it of downloading pirated books to train its AI models. A US court granted final approval in July 2026. The agreement covers more than 480,000 works allegedly obtained from pirate libraries, including Library Genesis and Pirate Library Mirror.The settlement followed a distinction drawn by a federal judge in 2025, which said that using copyrighted books to train AI models could qualify as fair use, but making and retaining copies of pirated books was not protected by that finding.However, the settlement did not establish that all AI training using copyrighted material is illegal.Researcher’s ‘end of the world’ warningIn September, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that AI developers were racing towards self-improving superintelligence without adequately addressing the risks. Coxon, who said he had worked on pretraining research at OpenAI and Anthropic, wrote that companies were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”.He said people building the technology believed it could “kill us all by the end of the decade”. His comments were a warning about future risks, not evidence that existing AI systems have reached that level of capability. His resignation fuelled debate over whether AI development should slow until safeguards improve.Claude and the Venezuela raidAnthropic faced questions after reports that the US military had used Claude during the January 3 operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.The Wall Street Journal reported that the model was used in the mission, but Reuters said it could not independently verify the report. Axios also reported its use during the active operation, while noting that the precise role was unclear.Anthropic said it could not comment on whether Claude had been used in a specific classified operation. The reports drew attention because the company’s restrictions on military use were already at the centre of its dispute with the Pentagon. The tasks Claude performed during the raid have not been publicly established.Changes to AI safety commitmentsAnthropic’s safety policies have also come under scrutiny. In February 2026, it substantially rewrote its Responsible Scaling Policy, introducing Frontier Safety Roadmaps and regular risk reports. In July, it changed internal access rules for unredacted risk reports, requiring them to be shared with at least 200 employees rather than all staff with regular security clearance.In October, the company retired a roadmap goal for systematic oversight of training data to assess alignment with Claude’s Constitution. Anthropic said existing reviews were already identifying the issues such checks were designed to catch, and that a later sample review found no additional problems. articles.title: US maritime agency warned Iran blockade was adding to rising Gulf premiums
articles.summary: US Maritime Administration acknowledged naval blockade’s impact on insurance premiums and cargo capacity, memo shows.
articles.body:
The United States government’s maritime agency flagged the disruptive impact of Washington’s blockade of Iran on commercial shipping in an internal memo, documents obtained by Al Jazeera reveal.

In an alert, the US Maritime Administration (MARAD) acknowledged the Iran war’s negative impact on insurance premiums and cargo capacity after US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced that it had disabled a Panama-flagged bulk carrier for attempting to breach the blockade.

MARAD administrator Stephen M Carmel shared the alert with a subordinate on October 12, following CENTCOM’s attack on the vessel Ocean Molica and unattributed attacks on three other tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz.

“Why it matters: This materially escalates the previous alert: merchant ships now face kinetic action from both sides, and the threat has spread to Gulf anchorages and the Gulf of Oman,” said the memo, titled “Alert – Hormuz risk expands beyond the strait”.

“That increases the likelihood of further war-risk premium spikes, crew refusals and effective tanker capacity contraction.”

Carmel shared the alert with MARAD colleague Michael Yarrington in an email requesting information about the impact of the attacks on insurance premiums and an update on the agency’s efforts to “rebuild” war risk insurance.

It is unclear whether the alert originated within MARAD or another agency.

“How is the insurance market responding to all this?” Carmel wrote to Yarrington, an official at MARAD’s Office of Marine Insurance.

Yarrington replied that a colleague had reached out to contacts in London for information and forwarded a summary of rising insurance premiums compiled from news reports.

Yarrington also shared a description of “core deliverables” considered crucial to MARAD’s work on war risk insurance, the details of which were redacted from the emails before their release.

Al Jazeera obtained the documents through a Freedom of Information Act request to MARAD, which is responsible for promoting the US maritime industry.

MARAD, which sits under the US Department of Transportation, the White House, the Department of Defence and CENTCOM, did not respond to requests for comment.

The emergence of the memo acknowledging the negative fallout of the blockade comes as a definitive end to the Iran war remains elusive after months of on-again, off-again negotiations between Washington and Tehran.

US President Donald Trump last week dismissed the need for a peace deal with Iran, days after suggesting that the conflict could end “fairly soon” and that renewed US strikes were “highly unlikely”.

“Those days have long since passed,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

Todd Huntley, a retired US Navy captain who leads the National Security Law Program at Georgetown University Law Center, said MARAD’s monitoring of the blockade was likely aimed at informing its advice to other branches of the US government.

“As far as I know, MARAD will issue general alerts on incidents or threats, but will not then discuss the consequences, eg, increases in insurance rates,” Huntley told Al Jazeera.

“I do think that some US officials either didn’t consider this risk or ignored it when ordering and implementing the blockade.

“To me, it was pretty obvious this was a likely development given past Iranian actions and threats.”

Ian Ralby, the CEO and founder of maritime security consultancy I.R. Consilium, said the Trump administration appeared to be less concerned about the “strategic considerations” of the blockade than preventing ships from contributing to Iran’s economic survival.

“The President has made it clear that he is unperturbed by the global economic fallout from the War – including the blockade – so it may also be the case that the potential consequences of the blockade were considered but dismissed as unimportant,” Ralby told Al Jazeera.

Global shipping has been roiled by attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28.

Some 130 attacks on vessels have been recorded in the region since the start of the conflict, resulting in the deaths of at least 25 seafarers, according to the International Maritime Organization (IMO).

October was the worst month for shipping since the war began, with 35 vessels targeted, according to the IMO.

While most attacks during the war have been blamed on Iran or Iranian-aligned forces, CENTCOM has claimed responsibility for destroying or disabling at least two dozen vessels, some of which it has identified as belonging to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) shadow fleet.

The turmoil in the strait has sharply driven up costs for shipping lines.

The cost of insurance for an oil tanker carrying crude from the Middle East to East Asia surged about 200-fold from January to the end of October, reaching $12.29 per barrel, according to the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).

As of July, insurers charged 3.5 percent–7.5 percent of a vessel’s market value for war risk cover, up from 0.10-0.25 percent before the war, according to industry estimates cited in the Parliament of Singapore, a major logistics and shipping hub.

Amid rising shipping costs, prices of crude oil and fertiliser have surged as much 60 percent and 112 percent, respectively, at various points during the war.

Boon Chuan Lim, an independent researcher in Singapore whose research on the turmoil in the Strait of Hormuz has been published in the Borsa Istanbul Review, said it was noteworthy that the Trump administration had placed enforcement of the blockade alongside other attacks when assessing disruption risk.

“A disabling strike adds a potential source of loss for vessels exposed to that enforcement, though the implications depend on each vessel’s circumstances,” Lim told Al Jazeera.

He added that danger was not limited to the narrow corridor in the strait.

“Geography matters, too,” Lim said. “Risk is not confined to the strait: Ships at anchor, bunkering or approaching ports can also be exposed.

“Insurance terms depend on the vessel, route, area and duration of exposure, so a wider threat can raise costs and complicate operations beyond the transit itself, but it does not mean every vessel faces the same additional premium.”

The Republicans’ crushing defeat in the US midterm elections on November 3 has been widely attributed to the fallout of the war, particularly higher fuel prices.

US Democrats achieved their best electoral performance in decades in a stinging rebuke of Trump ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Democrats have so far secured 56 seats in the 100-member US Senate and at least 257 seats in the 435-member House of Representatives.

articles.summary: Investing.com-- Bitcoin slumped to a near five-month low on Friday and was headed for a seventh straight week of losses as a debilitating rout in global arti...
articles.body:
Investing.com-- Bitcoin slumped to a near five-month low on Friday and was headed for a seventh straight week of losses as a debilitating rout in global artificial intelligence valuations left traders wary of any risky bets.

The world's largest crypto fell 2.8% to $61,999.4 by 05:31 ET (10:31 GMT), and was trading down 4.1% this week, extending a losing streak since early-October.

Broader cryptocurrency prices also fell on Friday as a wipeout in global tech valuations offered little room for risk-driven, speculative plays.

Tech valuations were dumped heavily this week as investors questioned the long-term returns on the massive spending on AI in recent years, and whether said spending was even sustainable in the coming months.

Anthropic's (NASDAQ:ANT) bumper initial public offering did little to lift sentiment, with the stock ending well below intraday highs and losing more ground in premarket trade on Friday.

Anthropic was also seen drawing some liquidity from crypto plays, with institutional investors steadily dumping spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds this week.

Data from aggregator SoSoValue showed spot Bitcoin ETFs nursing outflows of $1.12 billion so far this week, their third straight week of over $1 billion in outflows.

Bitcoin and crypto markets are grappling with a storm of negative factors in recent weeks. Chief among them is the prospect of higher U.S. interest rates, with a host of economic prints and Federal Reserve commentary pointing to a rate hike in December.

Higher rates bode poorly for speculative assets like Bitcoin.

Adding to pressure on crypto was an uncertain regulatory outlook, after the U.S. Democratic party swept both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections.

Markets feared a less favorable regulatory environment when the Democrats take office in 2027, with several top members of the party, most notably Senator Elizabeth Warren, having called for tighter crypto regulations.

articles.title: Nike pone a correr a todos sus deportes
articles.standfirst: La multinacional concentra sus recursos en cinco disciplinas en su nuevo plan estratégico • El negocio del running, que llegó a crecer más de un 20 % en un trimestre, marca la hoja de ruta
articles.summary: La multinacional concentra sus recursos en cinco disciplinas en su nuevo plan estratégico • El negocio del running, que llegó a crecer más de un 20 % en un trimestre, marca la hoja de ruta
articles.body: Apenas unas horas después de la victoria de Andreas Almgren en el maratón de Nueva York, Nike publicó un ingenioso mensaje sobre una foto de la celebración del atleta sueco, que viste y calza con el icónico Swoosh. El Get used to it ("ve acostumbrándote") no solo es un juego de palabras con su lema más universal, ‘Just do it’ ("simplemente hazlo"). También es una declaración de intenciones sobre cómo la multinacional norteamericana espera recuperar el terreno perdido frente a otras marcas: con el negocio del running como una de sus principales apuestas y con la idea de aplicar su fórmula a otros deportes. La compañía lo puso por escrito el pasado martes 17 de noviembre en su Día del Inversor, celebrado en su sede de Beaverton (Oregón). Allí presentó Full Stride Ahead ("Con paso firme") la estrategia con la que pretende volver a crecer. El plan concentra los recursos en cinco disciplinas prioritarias (running, entrenamiento, fútbol, baloncesto y outdoor) y en la división de moda deportiva, Sportswear, que agrupa Nike Sportswear, Jordan y Converse. Según las previsiones de la propia Nike, esas áreas, junto con 23 países considerados prioritarios, deberían generar más del 90 % del crecimiento de sus ingresos hasta 2031. “Estamos concentrando nuestros recursos allí donde tenemos mayor potencial para ganar”, resumió Elliott Hill, presidente y consejero delegado de la compañía. Para 2031, la empresa aspira a sumar unos 5.000 millones de dólares de ingresos respecto al ejercicio actual: unos 4.000 millones procederían de los deportes de alto rendimiento y otros 1.000 de Sportswear. La recuperación, sin embargo, no será inmediata según los cálculos de la propia multinacional. La compañía prevé que sus ingresos caigan este ejercicio en un porcentaje de un solo dígito alto y no espera crecer al mismo ritmo que el mercado hasta 2029. La piedra angular del plan es lo que Nike llama Sport Offense, una forma de organizar el negocio en torno a cada deporte, y el running ha sido -o está siendo- su banco de pruebas. En la conferencia con analistas del pasado 31 de marzo, Hill explicó que fue “el primer equipo en adoptar la estrategia”. Según desvelaba en Primavera, la sección de running desarrolló una propuesta de producto basada en las necesidades de los deportistas, segmentó la oferta según el canal de venta y reforzó su presencia en las tiendas con más storytelling (experienciales). El directivo cifró el resultado en un crecimiento superior al 20% en el trimestre: “Nike Running ha establecido así la hoja de ruta que deberán seguir las demás disciplinas deportivas”, avanzó entonces. Seis meses después, el 1 de octubre, Hill volvió a presentar el running como la punta de lanza de la compañía. Aseguró que el negocio “ha vuelto a crecer a doble dígito, con ganancias constantes de cuota de mercado” y que sumaba su sexto trimestre consecutivo al alza. Atribuyó parte de ese impulso a la franquicia Vomero, con la que, según dijo, Nike ha “prácticamente triplicado” su cuota en las zapatillas de máxima amortiguación. También anunció nuevos lanzamientos, entre ellos las Nike Apex, las 'superzapatillas' de competición con las que ganó Almgren en Nueva York, y que no llegarán a las tiendas hasta enero de 2027. La mejora llega después de un periodo en el que la marca cedió terreno en un mercado al alza. En 2025, las ventas de calzado de running crecieron un 8,9 % en Estados Unidos, según la firma de análisis de datos YipitData, y en ese mismo periodo la cuota de Nike en el calzado retrocedió tanto en las tiendas físicas como en internet. El mismo informe señala que esa cuota no fue a parar a un único competidor, sino que se repartió entre varias marcas, entre ellas Hoka, On, New Balance y Adidas. En la misma conferencia de octubre, Hill admitió que la compañía atraviesa “desafíos importantes”, aunque sostuvo que “no representan toda la realidad de Nike”. A continuación enumeró los deportes en los que, a su juicio, la nueva estrategia ya está dando resultados: el fútbol creció a doble dígito en las cuatro regiones gracias al Mundial, el entrenamiento creció a escala global y el baloncesto creció a doble dígito en Norteamérica. En esa misma lista, el consejero delegado incluyó dos deportes que ahora no están entre los prioritarios: “Tanto tenis como golf han crecido a doble dígito”. Tampoco aparecen entre las cinco disciplinas elegidas el fútbol americano ni deportes de equipo como el voleibol. El comunicado del Día del Inversor no detalla qué pasará con la inversión en ellos. La propia Nike advierte en ese documento que sus objetivos son previsiones sujetas a riesgos, como la ejecución de la estrategia, la competencia o los aranceles, y de que sus iniciativas “podrían no alcanzar los beneficios previstos”. Más o menos, como los que toma un atleta cuando se sitúa sobre la línea de salida de un maratón.

articles.title: AI wealth is already changing San Francisco's housing market
articles.summary: Down payments are rising in areas flush with AI and tech employers.
articles.body:
Thursday's blockbuster Anthropic ( ANT ) initial public offering created thousands of new millionaires, and that wealth is already transforming housing markets in San Francisco and the Bay Area.

Median down payments are rising in Northern California communities with the most AI and tech employers, according to an analysis by Realtor.com, a trend that started just before AI began seeing mass adoption in 2023.

In three counties where AI companies are particularly concentrated — San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara — the median homebuyer now makes a 25% down payment, up from a median of 20%-21% from 2020 to 2022. In contrast, median down payments have held steady at 20% in nearby counties with fewer AI employers.

In the pricey Bay Area, boosting a down payment by 5 percentage points means ponying up serious cash. The median home in the region costs $1.33 million, meaning the difference between a 20% and a 25% down payment is more than $60,000.

"Even as rates eased, buyers in some major markets continued to put more money down, which is consistent with AI and tech wealth changing who is buying homes," Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu said in a statement.

Renters are also feeling the effects of the boom. San Francisco, home to Anthropic and OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ), saw median asking rent jump 6.3% in October compared to a year earlier. In San Jose, it's up 6.2%. But nationally, rents were nearly flat.

Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance.

articles.title: My hometown voted Republican for 50 years. Then came an election shaped by economic frustration
articles.summary: If you find yourself in Colorado Springs, Colorado, do yourself a favor and head to the Mesa Overlook, where the red sandstone formations of the Garden of the Gods tower above the high-desert grasslands while the magnificent Pikes Peak stands watch.
articles.body: If you find yourself in Colorado Springs, Colorado, do yourself a favor and head to the Mesa Overlook, where the red sandstone formations of the Garden of the Gods tower above the high-desert grasslands while the magnificent Pikes Peak stands watch. It’s a one-of-a-kind view in a city that has no shortage of distinctive experiences. As someone who grew up there, I could go on and on about the landscape, the history, and just how good Red Top’s massive hamburgers were. As a former resident who visits frequently, I could share how much the city has changed and grown. And as a reporter covering the economy, I can relay how some residents of my hometown – like those in many other cities across the country – are enduring the financial gut punches that come with an energy price shock and five-plus years of high inflation. Those changes – in the city itself and in the increasing affordability concerns its residents face – help tell the story of why, for the first time in more than 50 years, my hometown elected a Democrat to Congress. A half-century first Colorado Springs has long been a conservative bastion. It’s a city with military installations to its north, east, south and southwest. It’s an evangelical hub, serving as the headquarters to ministries like Young Life and Focus on the Family. And while the 2026 midterm elections brought a slew of unexpected outcomes across the nation, the Colorado District 5 race still took me aback: Democrat Jessica Killin, who won 50.5% of the vote, unseated Republican Jeff Crank (who received 45.8%). Republicans have easily carried this district since it was formed in 1972. So, what changed this cycle? First, the Springs has been on a massive growth spurt since well before I was born. With its majestic purple mountains; its beautiful, spacious skies; and its wealth of other amenities, Colorado Springs has long attracted newcomers. In 1970, about 135,000 people lived there. It’s since tripled in size to a half-million people and could soon overtake Denver as Colorado’s largest city. (Denver, which is a consolidated city and county is more geographically limited.) But now, as Colorado Springs’ urban core is getting bigger and busier, the population mix is changing, said Steven Pittz, a political science professor at the University of Colorado Colorado Springs (UCCS). “In the past 10 to 15 years, we’ve had more young people moving (to the Springs) to be closer to that mountain lifestyle and a place that’s a little bit cheaper than Boulder, Denver, etc.,” he said. A growing, changing city The influx that Pittz referenced has been apparent on my visits home during that time. Of course, it feels like I’ve seen more out-of-state license plates or heard more mispronunciations of streets like Nevada, Tejon and Uintah; but many of my conversations and interactions have been with folks who moved to the Springs in the past 15 years. In the past couple of decades, I’ve witnessed open prairies be slowly overtaken by sprawling, cul-de-sac-laden subdivisions; the humble scrub oak on the face of Cheyenne Mountain be supplanted by million-dollar homes; and a lonely road on the east side of the Springs turn into a six-lane artery that now sits as the center of town. It’s the type of growth that you can just feel. But to be honest, it hasn’t seemed too out of place for Colorado Springs. The region has long served as a magnet: Thousands of years ago, it was a “cultural crossroads” for many indigenous tribes; in 1871, Colorado Springs was founded as a resort town, and, soon thereafter, became a health and wellness destination for tuberculosis patients; and by World War I, it started establishing itself as a military hub. A ‘sorting’ from red to purple The region has also changed through the realignment of Colorado’s congressional districts: District 5 went from including several conservative, rural counties to primarily El Paso County. It went from being a heavily Republican district to one where unaffiliated voters have the slight majority, followed by Republicans and then Democrats, Pittz said. He sees Colorado Springs and the Centennial State of Colorado being reflections of the “great sorting,” where people coalesce with others who align politically. Red states are becoming redder, blue states bluer, he said. “When I think about Colorado, and then I think about Colorado Springs,” he said, “there’s this question of, ‘How long do you remain a Republican stronghold in a state that continues to sort in that direction?’” Pittz said he wouldn’t be surprised if a Republican retakes District 5 in the next election cycle or two. However, he added, the 2026 race showed that it’s possible Colorado Springs could become a politically purple city (or at least a maroon one). For example, in 2024, President Donald Trump won the district by a relatively small margin; and in 2022, outgoing Democratic Governor Jared Polis carried the city, said John Suthers, a former Colorado attorney general and Republican who served as Colorado Springs’ mayor from 2015 to 2023. “For those of us who paid close attention, we realized that the demographics of the district had changed,” Suthers said. “Having said that, I will tell you, Jessica Killin won because it was a referendum on (President) Donald Trump.” At the heart of that referendum, Suthers said, were the negative consequences from two of Trump’s major decisions: tariffs and a war with Iran. “I’m not the most economically sophisticated person in the world, but I’m economically sophisticated enough to know that tariffs drive up prices,” Suthers said, adding they also run counterintuitive to Republicans who embraced free enterprise and free trade. “Small businesses are impacted by that, and everybody felt that.” “Then, all of a sudden, next thing you know, we’re in a war with Iran … and all of a sudden, we’re paying $4.60 for a gallon of gas,” he added. The negative economic sentiment caused a shift in the political winds among many in the Springs. And that included Suthers’ own Republican-heavy neighborhood nestled at the foothills of the Rocky Mountains where Killin’s yard signs outnumbered Crank’s by three to one, he said. “The Democrats were highly, highly motivated,” Suthers said. “But I know there were Republican neighbors of mine who said, ‘I’m through, and we’re voting Democrat.’ And if you talk to them, it was all economics.” Financial triage When you grow up in a single-parent family that’s hugging the poverty line, it’s easy to recognize some actions undertaken by those struggling to make ends meet. There’s a financial triage that occurs. First goes the discretionary spending. That includes nixing the already modest summer trip up I-25 to Denver to see the zoo, or the museum, or the fantastically unique Casa Bonita. Also, dining out becomes a luxury, and Olive Garden and Outback become special-occasion-only locales. And it doesn’t take too long for the belt-tightening to show up at the gas station – a $10 check would be cut to put enough in the tank to make it to payday; or at the grocery store – where shopping lists shrank and mental math took place the register; or to the discount retailer – where sales were scoured to get one new item to add to last year’s wardrobe. The hope is that the cuts made along the way prevent a deeper wounding. But sometimes, not even the electric bill, the insurance statement or the mortgage were safe. This type of pain and these types of actions aren’t always visible to outsiders. However, with each trip back home, I’ve noticed more potential signs that residents are experiencing increased financial strain: At the supermarket checkout, I witnessed a customer put back a box of cereal and a tube of ground beef, relegating the items from ‘nice to have’ to ‘cannot afford.’ At the gas station, the pump totals – $10 even, $20 even, $7 even — tell a story of drivers putting just enough gas in their tanks to get by. But beyond the decisions at the grocery store and the minimal fuel fill-ups, it’s also the foot-traffic dropping off at certain stores and restaurants, the longer lines at the food banks, and the increase in folks experiencing homelessness. Even as Colorado Springs’ population is growing and the economy is expanding, the city was short 27,700 housing units in 2023 and has a need for 60,000 more by 2035, a recent city assessment showed. Household budgets were running short as well: Roughly two-thirds of renters and homeowners are spending more than 30% of their income on housing costs. Unsurprisingly, cost-of-living concerns were front and center on the campaign trail this election, Killin told CNN in an interview. “Just like we’re hearing across the country, people here in El Paso County, they’re struggling,” she said in an interview days after her victory. “This is still a relatively affordable place compared to the rest of the Front Range in Colorado, but it’s growing increasingly unaffordable.” And it wasn’t just housing, said Killin, a fourth-generation Coloradan who grew up in the Springs. Rising healthcare costs, childcare costs, and business costs were weighing on people, she noted. And in the military-centric Springs, many veterans’ cost-of-living concerns were compounded by negative sentiment about the Iran war and its potential effects on national security and ally relationships, said Killin, an Army veteran herself. But above all, people told her that they feel like they can’t get ahead, she said. “They feel like the American Dream isn’t in reach anymore, and they want an economy that works for more people, not just the lucky few,” she said.

articles.title: Gap stock pops as the retail giant warns
articles.summary: Gap takes a more measured approach on its business as the holidays kick into gear.
articles.body:
The warm fall weather hasn't been kind to Gap ( GAP ).

Shares of the owner of Gap, Old Navy, Banana Republic and Athleta rose 3% in premarket trading as investors shrugged off a mixed quarter and focused on improved sales at Old Navy and continued strength at Gap.

Third-quarter sales rose 2% to $4 billion, while comparable sales were flat.

Adjusted earnings came in at 82 cents a share, topping estimates of 78 cents.

Comparable sales at the Gap brand jumped 9%, marking 12 straight quarters of gains.

Old Navy comparable sales were flat, improved from a 4% drop in the second quarter as the company course corrected on its assortments.

Banana Republic fell 3%, and Athleta continued to be a challenge as seen in a 15% sales drop.

But warmer fall weather softened demand in October and early November, forcing Gap to slash its full-year sales outlook to roughly flat from prior guidance for 1% to 1.5% growth.

The company also cut its adjusted earnings forecast to $2.29 to $2.34 a share from $2.35 to $2.45.

"We view 3Q as mixed, with Gap Inc. delivering better-than-expected profitability and sequential improvement at Old Navy, while Gap brand momentum remained strong. However, softer October/early November demand drove lower FY26 sales and profit guidance, with added promotions weighing on 4Q GM. We see encouraging underlying progress, but holiday execution remains key," Jefferies analyst Corey Tarlowe said.

articles.title: Anthropic's IPO ties the fate of the US economy closer to AI
articles.summary: Another mega tech company will have the power to steer everyone else's financial standing, for good and for bad.
articles.body:
The day finally arrived. Anthropic ( ANT ) began trading on Thursday at $111.50 per share, surging above its $83 IPO price and briefly attaining a market capitalization of $2 trillion before settling into a still-respectable $1.2 trillion. What took years for the tech giants to achieve, the frontier AI lab grabbed in an instant .

But the historic IPO is notable not just for its size , but also for what it says — and will say — about the makeup of the stock market and the outsized influence of its largest players.

The top 10 biggest companies make up close to 40% of the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ). A bad day for tech means a bad day for the market. And now that Anthropic has joined the trillion-dollar ticker club — though it won't join the S&P 500 anytime soon — Wall Street's fate is tightly bound with another huge tech company, which also happens to be an AI lab without a long track record of financial stability.

The top-heavy nature of the S&P 500 means the benchmark index is less diverse than it looks. Sure, investors are buying into a basket of hundreds of names. But since the tickers with the largest market caps get the highest proportional weights, a handful of names can move the entire index.

That's how you can get such different performances from the equal-weighted S&P 500 ( ^SPXEW ) index (up 11% so far this year) versus the standard, market-weighted version (up 6%).

Big Tech's importance in the stock market has attracted praise and concern for years, even before the arrival of ChatGPT. AI has only deepened that concentration. The tech giants have adopted the AI boom as their new reason for being. And, in a very literal sense, have poured huge investments into their own AI operations and a sprawling ecosystem of chipmakers, LLM suppliers, power generators, and infrastructure firms.

Anthropic's IPO adds to tech's significance and amplifies the industry's financial gravity. But the frontier lab is also a primary supplier of AI tools. And it counts the country's biggest tech firms as its biggest customers, as well as plenty of other major corporate services. That further intertwines the stock market's top players.

This recent drama over cyber outages and stories about urgent patches causing havoc also showcases AI tools in action and their myriad risks . And how they're integrated into the economy now — whether companies and users are ready for them.

And, of course, Anthropic's debut is only the beginning. OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) is coming, and the data center infrastructure boom is still accelerating, further pushing AI chips into the economy's pot. Should the AI boom underdeliver, all that concentration and interconnection will accentuate an AI disappointment into something far bigger.

articles.title: Anthropic's IPO winners and losers, from Ashton Kutcher to Sam Bankman-Fried
articles.summary: Ashton Kutcher and Sam Bankman-Fried both bet early on Anthropic. Only one is celebrating its public market debut.
articles.body:
Ashton Kutcher and Sam Bankman-Fried both bet early on Anthropic. Only one is celebrating its public market debut.

Bankman-Fried's FTX put $500 million into Anthropic ( ANT ) in 2021 for about 14% of the AI lab. After FTX collapsed, the estate sold the stake in 2024 for about $1.3 billion. Among the buyers was Jane Street, the trading firm where Bankman-Fried got his start.

That stake was worth more than $40 billion at Anthropic's first-day close of $97.17 — even after the stock opened at $111.50 , 34% above its $83 IPO price, and gave back part of the pop. Bankman-Fried, who is serving a 25-year sentence, told the New York Times from prison that he tries not to dwell on it. "There's no point in obsessing over regrets," he said. "But it's certainly something that I've spent, despite that, a fair bit of time thinking through."

Kutcher, meanwhile, had a different response : "Kind of cool," the actor said of the IPO on X. Sound Ventures, the firm he co-founded with Madonna's manager Guy Oseary, first backed Anthropic in 2023. Its $435 million turned into about $6 billion by the close, with some outlets reporting that the debut could make Kutcher a billionaire , despite his recent exit from the firm . NBA star Tristan Thompson is another celebrity backer, and he isn't selling .

Anthropic's seven co-founders were worth about $163 billion combined at the close, or more than $23 billion apiece, by Yahoo Finance calculations. They were the only insiders selling in the IPO, at about $280 million each.

The seven have pledged to give away 80% of their stock. That's about $130 billion at the close, more than the Gates Foundation's entire $92 billion endowment. The filing calls the pledges "voluntary, revocable," and the seven keep 50.1% of the vote either way.

Employees did fine as well. Their options and restricted stock were worth about $270 billion at the close. The average option costs just $2.91 a share to exercise, on a stock that closed at $97.17.

Amazon ( AMZN ) has put in $18 billion, and its roughly 15% stake was worth $190 billion at the close. Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL ) owns about 14%, worth about $175 billion. Nvidia ( NVDA ) had the quickest payday, turning a $10 billion buy at the IPO price into a gain of about $1.7 billion by the close.

Anyone who chased the open came up short, down about 13% by the close. Pricing 980 million shares at $83 left nearly $14 billion on the table, just shy of SpaceX's record $14.4 billion in University of Florida professor Jay Ritter's data . Its bankers didn't, with Goldman Sachs ( GS ) and Morgan Stanley ( MS ) set to collect about $113 million each .

articles.title: Hallmarked gold faces a purity test as India Bullion and Jewellers Association has flagged alleged adulteration using rhenium powder, fabricated gold purity reports through jeweller-hallmarking centre collusion and fee kickbacks
articles.summary: Gold prices are crashing and if you think this is a good time to buy jewellery, be alert about hallmarking in gold.
articles.body: Gold prices are crashing and if you think this is a good time to buy jewellery, be alert about hallmarking in gold. Concerns have emerged over the credibility of India’s BIS certification system following allegations of widespread irregularities in gold hallmarking and refining.The India Bullion and Jewellers Association (IBJA) has raised suspicions of collusion between jewellers and hallmarking centres, fabricated purity reports, kickbacks linked to fees and sophisticated methods of adulterating gold using rhenium powder, according to an ET report.Gold hallmarking concernsIn a representation submitted to the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), the association highlighted discrepancies in Hallmark Unique Identification (HUID) data displayed on the BIS Care app, along with the operations of unregistered refiners.It warned that shortcomings in regulatory monitoring could leave consumers vulnerable to financial losses and weaken confidence in hallmarked gold. The IBJA has called for surprise inspections, stricter testing procedures and stringent action against hallmarking centres and refiners found violating the rules.Following the industry body’s representation, the BIS has convened a meeting on November 23 to discuss the concerns in detail.India consumes around 800-850 tonnes of gold annually.The IBJA has also called on the BIS to bring nearly 4,000 unregistered gold refiners operating in India under its regulatory oversight. It alleged that the lack of supervision over these entities is enabling impure gold to enter the jewellery supply chain, creating the possibility of such gold reaching consumers.Surendra Mehta, national secretary of the India Bullion and Jewellers Association (IBJA), told ET that numerous businesses operating as gold refiners were neither registered with the BIS nor answerable to any regulatory body.He alleged that many of these operators were merely melting gold rather than refining it, resulting in impure metal entering the market through jewellers as gold bars, coins and jewellery.“These unregistered refiners make impure gold and operate in the same way fake currency notes are made and circulated,” Mehta said, stressing the need for stricter oversight of the gold refining industry.The IBJA has urged the BIS to bring every unregistered refiner under its supervision. It has also called for jewellers to be allowed to source gold bars and coins only from refiners accredited by the BIS and the National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories. The association has advised consumers and investors to buy gold bars and coins from accredited refiners to reduce the chances of purchasing adulterated gold.The representation comes against the backdrop of increasing industry concern over allegations that rhenium powder, reportedly sourced from China, is being mixed with gold to add weight to jewellery. There are concerns that this form of adulteration could go undetected during standard hallmarking checks, prompting questions about whether current testing procedures are adequate.The Gem & Jewellery Export Promotion Council (GJEPC) has also looked into the technical aspects of the alleged adulteration. It has written to the BIS seeking an official clarification on whether rhenium can be used to adulterate gold and whether hallmarking centres need to strengthen their testing methods.Rhenium is a refractory metal with a melting point of more than 3,100 degrees Celsius. At the temperatures typically used in jewellery manufacturing, around 1,050-1,100 degrees Celsius, it cannot melt or dissolve in gold.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: The post earnings slide in Nvidia stock is getting uglier by the day
articles.summary: The Nvidia sell-off refuses to let up in the post Jensen Huang era.
articles.body:
The Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock rout after earnings refuses to let up.

Shares of the fallen AI chip darling are down more than 10% since the company's Nov. 17 earnings report. The stock is down 14% since founder Jensen Huang resigned on Nov. 12 under a cloud of controversy, notably over his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Interim CEO and longtime CFO Colette Kress made a pretty compelling case this week that Nvidia can keep running the AI money machine without Huang in the driver's seat.

The earnings numbers were enormous. The outlook was ahead of estimates. And Kress came across as a steady operator who knows this business inside and out.

Nvidia delivered $2.68 in adjusted earnings per share on $115.8 billion in revenue. Wall Street was looking for $2.47 and $109.15 billion.

The next-quarter forecast? Revenue of $127.4 billion to $132.6 billion. Again, comfortably ahead of expectations.

And Nvidia now sees fiscal 2028 revenue growth of 75%, up from the 70% forecast just three months ago. The AI spending machine is showing no signs of slowing down — at least, that's the story Kress pitched.

But here's where the story gets messy, and why the stock is likely getting drilled.

New Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones stumbled badly on the leadership question on the earnings call. Investors wanted urgency. They wanted a clear timeline for finding a permanent CEO. Instead, they got a message that left the door open to an extended interim arrangement.

That's a problem. Nvidia is the company at the center of the biggest technology boom in a generation. Wall Street doesn't want a leadership guessing game.

Kress proved she can handle the numbers. Jones still has to prove the board can handle succession to one of the most celebrated tech founders in decades. And right now, that may be Nvidia's biggest unanswered question.

"I don't know that any internal candidate, though, is capable of running the whole company," Seaport Research Partners analyst Jay Goldberg said on Sozzi Unleashed . "Jensen famously built the structure of the company around himself. Like he's the center of the wheel and all the things connect to him. And I don't think anyone internally has as complete a view of the company as Jensen does."

Brian Sozzi is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, host of the Sozzi Unleashed morning show, the ' Power Players With Brian Sozzi' podcast and a member of Yahoo Finance's editorial leadership team.

articles.title: Is Wonder the dinner company for our anti-social times?
articles.summary: Dinnertime in America once looked like a family gathering around the table to eat mom’s cooking. Then came restaurants, fast food and takeout.
articles.body: Dinnertime in America once looked like a family gathering around the table to eat mom’s cooking. Then came restaurants, fast food and takeout. Now, when people still do get together for dinner, food delivery company Wonder wants them to eat their own personal portions of Thai, Japanese and Mediterranean. Wonder represents the extreme crackup of sharing a meal in America. The company offers more than two dozen types of cuisines —some from recognizable restaurant names and celebrity chefs — cooked out of roughly 170 storefronts it has opened in the Northeast in three years. Wonder has also bought Grubhub and Blue Apron, and it lists its individual brands like Limesalt on delivery apps. Wonder promises a kind of food abundance for families and friends struggling to agree on what to order for dinner: “the destination for every craving without compromise.” But ordering Chinese with friends when you’re in the mood for Mexican is not a problem that needs to be solved. It’s a normal part of being human. By the time you’re passing around dumplings and noodles, you’ll forgot you wanted tacos. At a moment when many consumers crave authenticity and community in an isolated, tech-fueled world, Wonder is offering steaks with Bobby Flay’s name on them mass prepared offsite and finished in nondescript “food halls” that look like an AI mashup of Sweetgreen and Starbucks. Speedy delivery and sleek branding are what matters above all, Wonder is betting. Wonder is not about the “community-based, squishy, ephemeral things” associated with food, said Lilly Jan, a chef and assistant teaching professor in the Cornell SC Johnson College of Business. “It’s a fast-fashion model for restaurants.” Wonder, valued at $9 billion and heading toward an IPO, says it’s bringing high-quality food to the suburbs and less densely-populated parts of the country where some individual restaurants couldn’t survive economically. It also offers lower prices than most delivery apps, zero fees and overnight options. “We believe a shared meal is about sitting down and spending time together, not about everyone eating the same thing,” a Wonder spokesperson said. “Wonder lets everyone get something they love and still eat together.” ‘Restaurants as software’ Wonder is the brainchild of Marc Lore, the master of online shopping. Lore founded Diapers.com and Jet.com. He started Wonder in 2018 as a so-called ghost kitchen offering different cuisines out of food trucks. The company pivoted to brick-and-mortar storefronts after the pandemic. Wall Street is high on Lore’s vision and Wonder’s cost-cutting technology. The company has developed a robot that can make about 500 bowls an hour, Lore has said. Investors also see potential in Wonder Create, a new program that lets anyone launch a restaurant on Wonder’s platform without paying for rent or labor. “Restaurants in our world are just software,” Lore said of Wonder Create. “They’re brands, logos and recipes that plug into the platform.” But many consumers are already fed up with AI-generated food images on menus and in advertising — “AI slop menus,” as some TikTokers have dubbed them. Vandals recently graffitied a San Francisco restaurant that used AI-generated images of bacon, egg and cheese sandwiches. Any takers for ChatGPT-designed restaurants? The idea of eating with a group of people at a restaurant with some character still matters to many people. Restaurants are a place to gather, try new foods and explore. They’re connected to a place and make up the fabric of neighborhoods. Wonder strips away the traditional relationship between restaurant and customer and turns it into a commodity, said Stephen Zagor, a restaurant consultant who teaches at Columbia Business School. That’s why some foodies and locals worried about the future of neighborhood restaurants have been unusually hostile online to Wonder’s arrival. The 300,000-member r/FoodNYC subreddit has become a place for people to gripe about Wonder popping up in their backyard, where there are too many restaurant options to count. Many of the comments go beyond the usual criticism of a restaurant’s food, or puzzlement over why anyone in New York City would order Wonder’s Thai instead of calling the neighborhood Thai joint 10 minutes away. Wonder says it’s not trying to replace restaurants and takes customer criticism seriously. But some of the pushback online reflects a deeper frustration with the homogenization and automation of American dining, symbolized by the growing presence of Wonder storefronts. “The thing about Wonder that I keep coming back to is its total lack of a reason to exist,” the writer Laura Ault said in a scathing piece about the company in the independent news outlet New Caananite in March. “Save for yet another late-stage capitalism ‘disruption’ plot.”

A gold investment can add stability and inflation protection to your portfolio. But it can also dilute your gains when stock prices are rising quickly. Finding the right balance between gold's diversification benefits and profiting from growth potential in other assets can be challenging.

Even the experts are divided on how to achieve the correct balance. Below, five experts explain their recommended gold allocations, which range from 0% to 20%.

Robert R. Johnson, professor at Creighton University's Heider College of Business, does not advocate gold investing. In his words, "while having a small position in precious metals may dampen portfolio volatility in the short-run, the tradeoff between slightly dampened volatility and the lost long-term return is certainly not a prudent one, particularly for Gen Z/millennials with long investing time horizons."

2% to 5% allocation, depending on the situation

Brett Elliott, director of content and SEO at American Precious Metals Exchange (APMEX), recommends setting an allocation that aligns with your investing goals.

Growth-oriented investors may be comfortable with an allocation of 10% or 15%, according to Elliott. But income investors will prefer a smaller position, because gold provides no yield. A 2% to 5% gold allocation can provide some resiliency without an excessive drag on income potential.

Blake McLaughlin, executive vice president at Axcap Ventures, said historical data support a gold allocation of 5% to 8%. "Gold may not offer the outsized return potential of private investments, but the metal holds a set of attributes that are increasingly hard to ignore," according to McLaughlin. Those attributes include the metal's resilience amid economic uncertainty and geopolitical unrest.

Thomas Winmill, portfolio manager at Midas Funds, believes most investors will benefit from a long-term gold allocation of 5% to 15%. Winmill specifically advocates investing in gold mining companies through a mutual fund.

Your risk tolerance and current mix of financial versus hard assets can guide you to an appropriate allocation, according to Winmill.

Risk tolerance: Keep your allocation percentage low if you tend to panic in volatile cycles.

Financial vs. hard assets: Financial assets are stocks and bonds. Hard assets include tangible items like real estate, gold, collectibles, classic cars, and equipment. If you have no home equity and your wealth is primarily in financial assets, you can set your gold allocation higher. Or, if your home is paid for and more valuable than your stock portfolio, gold investing may not be necessary.

Vince Stanzione, CEO and founder at First Information, recommends a 20% gold allocation, specifically in physical gold or a gold ETF. Stanzione argues for a higher exposure to gold as a wealth protection strategy. As he says, "gold keeps with inflation and gold retains its purchasing power," while paper currencies are devaluing around the world.
